http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/14/russi.text: A Russian court has sentenced Georgy Pirogov to 23 years in a high-security penal colony for spying for Polish intelligence, with the FSB announcing the verdict the day after Poland said it had detained a Russian national suspected of planning a killing in Warsaw.The FSB said Pirogov left Russia after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, established contact with a representative of Polish military intelligence in Poland in April 2022, and was then tasked with collecting and passing classified information about Russian weapons used in the war.The FSB's statement did not explain when or how Pirogov returned to Russia or provide any evidence to back its claims.On Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a Russian citizen had been detained on 7 August on suspicion of preparing an assassination in Warsaw.Tusk said Russian security services had recruited the suspect and added that the Kremlin chose the intended target because it saw him as a threat."He was inconvenient from the point of view of Putin's regime," Tusk said. The Polish premier declined to name the target, citing legal restrictions.Pirogov's trial opened in May and was held behind closed doors. The FSB said he used contacts in Russia's defence industry to obtain restricted information on the production and use of missile systems, as well as personal data of individuals with access to state secrets.The indictment also alleged he made cryptocurrency transfers to support Ukraine's armed forces, bought equipment and organised its delivery from Poland to Ukraine.The independent Russian outlet Mediazona reported that Pirogov moved to Georgia after the invasion began and worked as an industrial climber, citing relatives and human rights activists. In the summer of 2024 he travelled to Uzbekistan on a business trip and then disappeared.In July 2024 it emerged he was being held at Matrosskaya Tishina remand prison in Moscow. Independent Russian media said they did not know who detained him or under what circumstances he was brought back to Russia.Treason charges a tool of the KremlinRussia has significantly expanded its espionage and treason laws since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.The maximum sentence for treason rose from 20 to 25 years after legislative changes in 2022 and 2023, and the definition of state treason was broadened to cover a wider range of contacts with foreign states and organisations.The FSB has also been given expanded powers to detain and prosecute individuals suspected of espionage without the same evidentiary threshold previously required.Treason cases in Russia numbered in the single digits annually before 2014, when Russia's initial invasion of Ukraine and annexation of Crimea prompted the first significant spike.Last year, almost 500 people, including Ukrainian citizens, were convicted in Russia on espionage and treason charges.Since Russia's full-scale invasion, Poland has become one of Ukraine's most significant military supporters, providing weapons, ammunition and training. Poland also hosts a large US military presence.Warsaw has expelled Russian diplomats and closed the Russian consulate in Kraków over espionage concerns.Poland's counter-intelligence services have reported a major increase in Russian malign interference, including sabotage and recruitment operations on Polish soil since 2022, targeting infrastructure, Ukrainian diaspora networks and individuals critical of the Kremlin.

https://www.tmz.com/2026/09/04/andrew-ta.text: Andrew and Tristan Tate have been indicted on multiple charges in Romania. Romania's Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism announced the indictment on Friday ... stating that it stems from an investigation into two British men from the same family, aged 39 and 38. Local media identified these two people as the Tate brothers. Andrew has been indicted for trafficking minors, money laundering, sex with a minor, and witness tampering, while Tristan was indicted for complicity. Prosecutors claim the Tates recruited the alleged victims in the case by claiming they wanted to be in a relationship with them or to marry them ... before allegedly forcing them to make pornographic content for a webcam business the two men ran together. One of the alleged victims was 15 years old when prosecutors say Andrew took her to Romania from the United Kingdom and forced her to make content. Tristan allegedly used physical aggression to coerce the woman. The Tates are said to have made more than $1 million via the content they allegedly made her produce. Prosecutors also claim they tried to launder that money by purchasing four luxury cars. The Tates' lawyer in Romania -- Eugen Vidineac -- said in a statement, "We will examine every aspect of [the indictment] with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process." It's unclear when the Tates may go to Romania to face the charges ... because they're still in the United States fighting extradition to the United Kingdom, where they each face numerous charges -- with more than 50 counts against Andrew and close to 20 against Tristan. According to reports, they can be tried in absentia in Romania once a judge signs off on the case moving forward.
